PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Presidential Decree 756 on the competency of the Ministry of Emergency Situations
DESCRIPTION: This document sets the responsibilities of the Ministry of Emergency Situations, notably with regard to natural disasters like fires.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Decree-Law No. 147 on the Reorganisation of Central State Administrative Organs (creation of Ministry of Sciences, Technology and Environment responsible for Climate Change policy)
DESCRIPTION: The Decree-Law abolishes the National Commission for Energy and other state bodies and transfers its functions to the Ministry of Economy and Planning and Ministry of Basic Industry. It further transforms the Academy of Science of Cuba into the Ministry of Sciences, Technology and Environment, and assigns it the responsibilities previously carried out by the National Commission for Protection of the Environment and the Rational Use of Natural Resources, the National Commission for Atomic Energy (established in 1979) and the Commission Responsible for the Grand National Park Sierra Maestra.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Rail Investment Plan
DESCRIPTION: In early 2025, Morocco's Minister of Transport and Logistics presented a MAD 96 billion investment plan to modernize the country's rail system by 2030. MAD 53 billion is earmarked for the construction of a high-speed rail line between Marrakech and Kenitra, MAD 29 billion to aquire 18 high-speed trains and 150 multi-service trains, and MAD 14 billion to build or renovate railway stations.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Brazil's Adaptation Climate Plan: Thematic Plan for Water Resources
DESCRIPTION: Brazil’s Thematic Plan for Water Resources aims to strengthen the resilience of the country’s water systems to climate change. The plan focuses on reducing vulnerabilities associated with changing rainfall patterns, droughts, floods, water scarcity, and extreme hydrological events that threaten water security, ecosystems, economic activities, and human well-being. The plan also emphasizes the sustainable management of water resources, nature-based solutions, coordination across sectors and levels of government, and the protection of water availability and quality under future climate conditions.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Vision 2030, The Chad We Want
DESCRIPTION: This document provides the strategic framework that underpinning the operational planning in Chad's National Development Plans. This framework comprises 4 axes: strengthening national unity; strengthening good governance and the rule of law; developing a diversified and competitive economy; and improving the quality of life of the Chad people.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Sida's Climate and Environment Policy
DESCRIPTION:
Sida is the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency, , a government agency that works to reduce poverty and promote development in other countries. This policy is part of Sida’s management system for climate and environment based on the Regulation for Environmental Management in Government Agencies (2009:907) and the Regulation for Government Climate Adaptation Work (2018:1428).This policy shall guide the formulation of Sida’s internal goals and proposals for strategic objectives that Sida proposes to the Swedish Government.

Sida's strategic areas are: climate adaptation and mitigation; sustainable use, restoration and conservation of forest, land, water and marine resources; and reduction of air, soil and water pollution.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Regulation on State Subsidies for Solar Panels - Regulation No. 2009:689, updated/ amended by Regulation no. 2011:1473
DESCRIPTION:
The Regulation on State Subsidies for Solar Panels provides for financial support to facilitate the uptake of solar installations. This regulation forms the basis of grants for all types of solar/PV installations. The solar/PV market in Sweden is predominantly focused on off-grid installations in homes in remote areas and utilities such as communication stations or lighthouses. Grid-connected facilities with solar/PV are mostly used for research or demonstration purposes. The regulation is aimed at private individuals, companies and municipalities.


In November 2011 the regulation was amended, which reduced the subsidies from 46% to a maximum of 43% of the eligible costs per installation from 1 February 2013 onwards. The total budget allocated to the 2013-2016 period is SEK210m (USD28.4m).

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: An Energy Policy for Europe
DESCRIPTION:
The point of departure for a European energy policy is threefold: combating climate change, limiting the EU's external vulnerability to imported hydrocarbons, and promoting growth andjobs, thereby providing secure and affordable energy to consumers. In this Strategic Energy Review the Commission proposes that the European Energy Policy be underpinned by:

• an EU objective in international negotiations of 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by developed countries by 2020 compared to 1990. In addition, 2050 global GHG emissions must be reduced by up to 50% compared to 1990, implying reductions in industrialised countries of 60-80% by 2050;

• an EU commitment now to achieve, in any event, at least a 20% reduction of greenhouse gases by 2020 compared to 1990.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Presidential Decree 15-334 on hosting the Pan-African University Institute for Water and Energy Sciences (27 December 2015)
DESCRIPTION: This is the Presidential Decree No. 15-334 of 15 Rabie El Aouel 1437, corresponding to 27 December 2015, ratifying the Host Agreement between the Government of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria and the African Union Commission for the hosting of the Pan-African University Institute for Water and Energy Sciences (Institut UPA), including Climate Change, signed in Algiers on May 29, 2014.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Just transition strategy 2021
DESCRIPTION: The Just Transition Strategy (ETJ), as part of Spain's Strategic Energy and Climate Framework, ensures a fair and inclusive ecological transition by creating quality jobs, supporting vulnerable communities, and promoting social and territorial cohesion. It focuses on gender equality, rural revitalization, stakeholder engagement, and sectoral planning while enhancing RD and innovation. Through "Just Transition Agreements", it aims to mitigate negative impacts on workers and regions, particularly coal-dependent areas, ensuring that the shift to a low-carbon economy drives economic growth and environmental sustainability without leaving anyone behind.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Decree No. 167/2017 to determine the minutes of application of Article 20 of the Law on Environmental Protection No.444 of 2002
DESCRIPTION: This decree notably grants preferential taxation levels to environmentally-friendly activities that include the renewable energy industry and other activities favouring energy efficiency.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Cap. 610 Buildings Energy Efficiency Ordinance
DESCRIPTION: Cap. 610 Buildings Energy Efficiency Ordinance  provides the legislative basis for the energy efficiency labelling of infrastructure. This Ordinance requires compliance with codes of practice in relation to energy efficiency of air-conditioning installations, electrical installations, lift and escalator installations and lighting installations. It also sets out energy audit processes for buildings.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: CONPES 3919/2018 - National Policy of Sustainable Building
DESCRIPTION: This policy aims to integrate sustainability into the life cycle of buildings by using transition tools, monitoring, control mechanisms, and financial incentives, targeting sustainable construction initiatives through 2025. The policy complies with the stipulations of the National Development Plan 2014-2018 "All for a New Country," deepening the vision of the National Green Growth Strategy and the sectoral mitigation action plan for housing and territorial development (2014), as part of the Colombian Low Carbon Development Strategy. Moreover, the policy supports international commitments like the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), focusing on sustainable cities (Goal 11), sustainable consumption and production (Goal 12), reducing GHG emissions (Paris Agreement), and following the New Urban Agenda set at Habitat III.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Decarbonization Plan - Government of Costa Rica 2018-2050
DESCRIPTION: National Decarbonization Plan - Government of Costa Rica 2018-2050, Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy from Costa Rica in 2019

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Renewable Energy Program
DESCRIPTION: This program aims to maximise the potential of renewable energy in the country. It sets the government's vision to diversify energy sources, stimulate sustainable growth and reduce GHG emissions.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Law No. 2023-900 of 23 November 2023 establishing the Environmental Code
DESCRIPTION:
The State shall prepare a report every five years on the state of the environment, including sectoral reports, relating to biodiversity, climate change, desertification, pollution levels, coastal areas, marine environments, and quality of life.

Environmental impact assessments are to take into account climate change.

The Code also contains a section on climate change, where the State is to adopt mitigation and adaptation strategies, promote technology transfer, publish reports every three years, and facilitate financing mechanisms.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Regulation (EU) 2019/2089 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2019 amending Regulation (EU) 2016/1011 as regards low carbon benchmarks
DESCRIPTION: This Regulation of the European Parliament and Council amends a 2016 regulation creating uniform rules for benchmarks in the Union and caters for different types of benchmarks used by financial market actors. The Regulation introduces provisions around the creation of EU Climate Transition Benchmarks, EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks and sustainability-related disclosures for benchmarks and empowers the Commission to create minimum standards for these benchmarks and sets out requirements that the administrators of such benchmarks must adhere to.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Submission by Transforma, iGST Latin America and the Carribean regional hub, Disclosure Insight Action (CDP) and Climate Analytics Carribean
DESCRIPTION: Submission by Transforma, iGST Latin America and the Carribean regional hub, Disclosure Insight Action (CDP) and Climate Analytics Carribean, Submission to the Global Stocktake from Transforma, External organization authors in 2023

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Myanmar Energy Master Plan 2015
DESCRIPTION:
The Myanmar Energy Master Plan has been prepared from a strategic perspective requiring that all concerned Ministries align to a common energy development plan based on an understanding of fundamental economic development needs.

The plan provides the supply strategies through viable energy mix scenarios to secure the stable and reliable energy supply in the long term view. Moreover, this master plan is developed to ensure the efficient use of energy resources, to create effective investment environment, to employ innovative technologies and to minimise the environment and social impacts.

The plan prioritises the long term benefit of the country by ensuring sustainable energy sector development and conserving the environment. The planning process is also designed to ensure the integration of Global and ASEAN commitments in Myanmar Energy Master Plan.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Action Plan for Combating Soil Erosion (2013-2017)
DESCRIPTION: This Action Plan for 2013-2017, issued by the Ministry of Forestry and Water Affairs, aims to combat erosion effectively across Türkiye, improve coordination among the public agencies involved, and use public resources efficiently. It responds to widespread erosion, which is active on about 59% of agricultural land, 64% of rangelands and 54% of forest land. Its objectives include reducing soil loss and flood risk, extending the life of dams, protecting water quality, increasing soil productivity, and building public awareness. The Action Plan covers four types of activity: erosion control, afforestation, and the rehabilitation of degraded forests and rangelands. It targets new work on 1.4 million hectares and maintenance on 2.287 million hectares of earlier sites. Progress will be tracked through a web-based system updated quarterly and coordinated by the General Directorate of Combating Desertification and Erosion.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Strategy and Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Agricultural Sector (SPN2A 2020-2035)
DESCRIPTION: The strategy aims to enhance planning capabilities and subsequent implementation in the country's agricultural sector. It guides the operationalisation of priority actions to improve resilience. The National Strategy for Adaptation of the Agricultural Sector to Climate Change corresponds to the sectoral version of the National Adaptation Plan (NAP). The strategy seeks to attract funds from international climate financing schemes.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Peru's National Territorial Planning Strategy (Estrategia Nacional de Ordenamiento Territorial)
DESCRIPTION: The "National Strategy for Territorial Planning of Sedatu 2020-2040" in Mexico aims to shape the spatial dimension of the country's development over the long term. It acknowledges the negative impacts of past urbanisation and housing policies, including increased regional inequalities, disordered urban sprawl, exploitation of natural resources, and ecosystem degradation. The strategy emphasises that climate change and inequality are critical challenges, and decisions regarding cities, territories, and resource use will have global consequences. Territorial Planning is presented as a public policy to reduce social inequalities, build more sustainable, safe, and inclusive settlements, and promote rational natural resource use.The strategy prioritises social-spatial justice, focusing on vulnerable groups and indigenous communities, ensuring safe environments with climate change adaptation capabilities. It seeks to strengthen climate change mitigation and adaptation measures, promote rational land use, and conserve ecosystem services for balanced, sustainable development across all regions. Key challenges addressed include promoting clean energy sources, fulfilling international commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and implementing sustainable waste management practices. The strategy also aims to reduce social vulnerability to disasters, improve basic services in urban and rural areas, and strengthen the capacity of municipalities to adapt to disaster risks related to natural phenomena by 2040.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Norway's climate action plan (Meld. St. 13 2020-2021)
DESCRIPTION: This document is the government's white paper laying out how it intends to meet its climate targets by 2030. It sets sectoral strategies of emissions reductions, notably with regard transport and the carbon tax. The government has proposed that it will increase the carbon tax to 2000 kroner per tonne of CO2 by 2030 on emissions not covered by the European ETS. The government has also introduced a tax on waste incineration.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Agroforestry Policy 2014
DESCRIPTION:
The National Agroforestry Policy establishes the framework of a focused national policy and a suitable institutional mechanism for the country. 

The major policy goals are: 1) setting up a National Agroforestry Mission or an Agroforestry Board to implement the National Policy by bringing coordination among various elements of agroforestry scattered in various existing missions, programmes, schemes and agencies pertaining to agriculture, environment, forestry, and rural development sectors of the Government; 2) improving the productivity; employment, income and livelihood opportunities of rural households, especially of the smallholder farmers through agroforestry; 3) meeting increasing demand of timber, food, fuel, fodder, fertilizer,fibre, and other agroforestry products; 4) conserving the natural resources and forest; 5) protecting the environment and providing environmental security; 6) increasing the forest / tree cover.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Regulation on Energy Performance in Buildings
DESCRIPTION: Turkey updated this Regulation to include near-zero energy building (NZEB) requirements with expanded thresholds (size of 2,000 m² from the previous 5,000 m²) requiring NZEB certification with Class B energy rating and minimum 10% renewable energy integration targeting 40% energy savings in buildings by 2030.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Small-Scale Renewable Electricity Generation Scheme (SRESS)
DESCRIPTION:
This Scheme helps farmers, community groups, schools, and businesses lower electricity costs and generate income through solar and wind projects.

  • The self-consumer grant, under the Non-Domestic Microgen Grant (NDMG) scheme helps those who want to install solar panels to power their farm, business, or community buildings. Renewable Self-Consumers above 50kW and up to 1MW are eligible to apply and receive up to €162,600.
  • The SRESS export tariff is for projects which export all electricity produced to the grid to earn income. The SRESS export tariff provides a 15-year tariff to successful export applicants, without an auction. The support rate is provided for the support lifetime, with successful applicants receiving a premium on the market revenues they receive for their renewable electricity.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Regulation on the tracking of greenhouse gas emissions
DESCRIPTION: The purpose of this Regulation is to regulate the procedures and principles for monitoring, reporting and verification of greenhouse gas emissions from specified activities, including the burning of fuels at thermal power plants, metal production, and pulp and paper industrial production. Businesses are obliged to prepare a greenhouse gas emission monitoring plan, a document on the detailed, complete and transparent documentation of data collection and data processing activities and their monitoring methodology, including the accuracy control system, 6 months prior to theinitial monitoring of greenhouse gas emissions. They are monitor their greenhouse gas emissions in accordance with the stipulated calculation, measurement, and reporting requirements, every year, with the submission on 30 April following each calender year.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Blue Economy Development Framework for Indonesia’s Economic Transformation
DESCRIPTION: Blue Economy Development Framework for Indonesia’s Economic Transformation provides a  basis for future blue economy policy planning and implementation in Indonesia. It notably assesses how to reduce the adverse impacts from climate change, decarbonise shipping and develop a low-emission economy.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Law no. 5069 of 2023. Conditions of building, construction, permitted land uses for data centres, zoning and urban planning regulations, utilisation of Green Fund resources, other environmental and energy provisions and other urgent provisions
DESCRIPTION:
The primary objective of the law is to establish a comprehensive framework for the conditions of building and construction, permitted land uses for data centres, zoning and urban planning regulations, and the utilisation of Green Fund resources. The law also includes other environmental and energy provisions and addresses urgent issues related to these areas.

Some of the key provisions included in the law are:

  1. Implementation of targeted measures for the development of renewable energy sources, including the installation of photovoltaic stations and wind farms.
  2. Measures and incentives should be provided to increase energy efficiency in urban planning, public buildings, infrastructure, and public facilities.
  3. The stipulation of mandatory flood protection and infrastructure restoration work to mitigate the impacts of climate change.
  4. It requires the preparation and implementation of local waste management plans that focus on reducing waste pollution.
  5. Measures for improving forest fire fighting and regulating logging operations for the installation of photovoltaic plants to protect forest areas and enhance their resilience to climate change should be included.
  6. Specific procedures for using Green Fund resources to finance actions and projects aimed at environmental protection and energy efficiency are outlined.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Regulation 180/2017 Energy efficiency requirements for goods and services in direct procurement organised by public authorities
DESCRIPTION: This Regulation determines the requirements to be set in procurements organised by direct administrative institutions regarding the energy efficiency of goods and services. Pursuant to the Section 55 of the Public Procurement Law, the minimum energy efficiency requirements for goods procured by state central administration institutions are stated: (1) correspondence to one of the highest two energy efficiency classes, available in the market (if EU labelling regulation applies); (2) correspondence to eco-design requirements (if EU eco-design regulation applies).

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Agreement on regulatory framework for CO2 storage in Denmark (2022)
DESCRIPTION:
In this agreement, a decision was taken ensure that the Danish state will be a co-owner of CO2 storage licenses in Denmark. The Danish subsoil is a shared resource, and state participation ensures that the state can have influence on subsoil activities related to CCS. State participation will also ensure that Danish society gets a share in any potential economic gains from CO2 storage.

The parties to the agreement furthermore decided that state ownership will be assumed by Nordsøfonden (the Danish State Subsurface Resource Company), which is deemed to have the necessary experience and competence from its engagement in oil and gas activities to protect the state's interests.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Strategic Contract for the Timber Sector 2023-2026
DESCRIPTION:
This Strategic Contract was signed between the Minister of Agriculture and Food Sovereignty, Christophe Béchu, Minister of Ecological Transition and Territorial Cohesion, Agnès Pannier-Runacher, Minister of Energy Transition, Roland Lescure, Minister Delegate in charge of Industry, Patrice Vergriete, Minister Delegate for Housing and industry partners in the timber sector. It has four priorities:

  1. The ecological transition;
  2. Reindustrialisation, sovereignty and competitiveness;
  3. Innovation and digitalisation; and
  4. The development of skills and attractiveness.

This Strategic Contact aims to amplify the decarbonising role of the forest-wood sector in climate-carbon neutrality strategies by implementing a sector-wide tool to map material and carbon flows. These projects will focus on developing destination markets for wood (material, fibers, molecules, energy) and adapting supply throughout the value chain, all the way to the forest, supporting the sector's contributions to major climate challenges.

The forestry and timber sector aims to contribute to the discussion and inform the authorities about its optimised contribution to the SFEC, and more generally to the low-carbon transition, based on a projection from 2018 to 2050. To this end, it plans to integrate all the data relating to its carbon potential for the climate (sequestration by forest sinks, storage and substitution by products through the use of wood materials, substitution by renewable energy from biomass) and, as a main output, to be able to describe a central future scenario for the sector's contribution.

Another aim is to take sustainable action to adapt forests, maintain their vitality, support the carbon pump, and produce timber, with a forest renewal and risk management plan.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Ghana REDD+ Strategy (2016-2035)
DESCRIPTION:
This Strategy has been designed to meet the requirements of the Warsaw Framework on REDD+ and other decisions of the Conference of the Parties of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) - it contains strategies on institutional arrangements; policy and legal frameworks; grievance mechanisms; and tracking. In developing the national REDD+ strategy, significant attention has been paid to national circumstances and developmental aspirations, and the process also took due cognisance of major national policies, including the national climate change policy (2013) and the revised forest and wildlife policy of Ghana (2012).

One of the goals of the Strategy is transforming Ghana's major agricultural commodities and Non Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) into climate-smart production systems and landscapes.

Countries that intend to undertake REDD+ (reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation in developing countries) activities are required to develop a national strategy that clearly articulates measures aimed at addressing the drivers of deforestation and forest degradation and other associated issues including land and tree tenure, forest governance, gender and safeguards.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Budget Law (climate tax on liquid fuels and tax rebate on low-carbon cars)
DESCRIPTION:
The budget law in Luxembourg has been related to climate change mitigation efforts for a number of years. In the budget 2018, the law of December 15th, 2017, stipulates in article 28 that the product of the climate change contribution levied on liquid fuels and its assignment to the Climate and Energy Fund can be charged on the revenue and expenditure budget. Article 29 states that the product of the road vehicle tax can be charged on the revenue and expenditure budget and be affected to the Climate and Energy Fund for 40 pr cent of the total.
 
 Article 129d of the budget law defines the conditions of tax rebate for the private ratepayer acquiring a new low-carbon vehicle. The "sustainable mobility rebate" applies to 1) zero-emissions cars functioning with electricity or fuel-cell hydrogen, 2) an electrically-assisted cycle, 3) a cycle registered after December 31st, 2016, and 4) a rechargeable hybrid car with emissions under 50 g CO2/km registered after December 31st, 2017.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Climate Change Action Plan for Ministry of Land Management, Urban Planning and Construction 2015-2018
DESCRIPTION:
The Climate Change Action Plan of Land Management creates a national and regulatory framework engaging the public, the private sector, and civil society through participatory process in an integrated land managemet, urban planning which can help to build resilience and sustainability through green infrastructure. 

The plan establishes the following key strategies : 1) to promote low-carbon, climate-resilient city development planning and develop city-level coordination mechanisms; 2) to promote land use planning, prioritize adaptation measures for key regions of Cambodia, such as coastal zones, highlands, rural and urban areas; 3) to promote low-carbon planning and technologies to support sustainable development though building code for buildings and infrastructure development; 4) to enhance capacity development for technical staff and awareness raising for rural publics on construction of traditional houses in rural area resilient to extreme climate change such as storms and floods.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Law no. 4964 of 2022 concerning provisions for the simplification of environmental licensing, establishing a framework for the development of Offshore Wind Farms and dealing with the energy crisis environmental and other provisions
DESCRIPTION:
The purpose of this law is to address serious and urgent issues concerning the protection of both the natural and urban environments, as well as to tackle the energy crisis. 

The subject addressed by the law includes:  

a) Simplifying environmental licensing and controls;  

b) Rationalising permitted land uses;  

c) Regulating the organisation and management of resources within the Natural Environment and Climate Change Organisation and the Green Fund;  

d) Addressing issues related to the protection of forests;  

e) Updating aspects of urban planning legislation;  

f) Establishing overall regulations for the development of offshore wind farms; and  

g) Managing issues associated with the energy crisis and promoting a circular economy.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Transport Sector Mitigation and Adaptation Plan
DESCRIPTION: Sectoral mitigation strategy and adaptation plan focused on reducing emissions from transport through electrification and modal shift. Key measures include expanding electric bus fleets in Santiago and other regions, electrifying taxis and shared taxis (“colectivos”), expanding metro and rail networks, and developing cycling infrastructure. Implementation of these measures is expected to deliver at least 3.43 MtCO₂e in emissions reductions by 2030.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Water Sector Strategy (2024-2035)
DESCRIPTION: Lebanon's National Water Sector Strategy (2024-2035) emphasises the importance of enhancing resilience to climate change in the country's water systems. By 2035 he strategy aims to: increase storage capacity; introduce a comprehensive digital monitoring system for national water usage and resources; increase hydropower production capacity by 15%; expand access and public management of water and wastewater systems; achieve a 30% energy cost reduction in the water sector through efficiency measures; and promote stronger governance in the water sector. Further adaptation-related measures include setting up a water resilience research program, and a stormwater management plan due to the increased incidence of extreme rainfall events under climate change.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Law on Disaster Prevention, 2003
DESCRIPTION:
This law regulates matters relating to the principles and full powers of disaster protection organizations and agencies, their organisation and activities, as well as the rights and duties of the State, local authorities, enterprises, entities and individuals in relation to disaster protection.

The law defines 'disaster protection' as the set of measures to prevent, protect and rescue people, livestock, properties and environment from the impact of disasters and to limit their consequences, to facilitate rapid recovery and to train the public for these activities. 'Disaster' means loss of many human lives and livestock, immense damage to property and environment caused by hazardous phenomena, major technological accident, terrorist acts or explosion.

The structure of disaster protection organisations is composed on the territorial-industrial principle regardless of the ownership in the state, Aimag, capital city, Soum, district, bag, khoroo, entities and enterprises. The state administrative organization in charge of disaster protection and their units, teams, branches and staffs in Aimags, capital cities and districts are responsible for the nation-wide implementation of the disaster protection activities. The unofficial services and specialised units are in administrative and territorial units. The entities, enterprises, bags and khoroos are responsible for disaster protection at the grassroots level.
The state administrative organisation in charge of disaster protection is the organisation responsible for the implementation of the state disaster protection policy and the legislation on disaster protection and the organisation of nation-wide disaster protection activities and is provided with professional management. The state administrative organisation in charge of disaster protection is set up and dissolved by the Government on the basis of the scheme approved by the Parliament.

The government shall submit the draft of disaster protection programme of Mongolia for the consideration of the Parliament, to take the measures in order to implement it. The State shall also finance centralised disaster protection activities. Disaster protection activities of the Aimag, capital city, Soum, district, bag, and khoroo are financed by local budget. Entities and enterprises shall be liable for expenses by own fund.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Decree No 2022 - 698
DESCRIPTION:
Decree No. 2022-698 establishes the procedures for registering carbon projects within the country. The Autorité d'Enregistrement des Projets Carbone (AEPC), or Carbon Project Registration Authority, is the government institution responsible for overseeing the implementation of this decree. The AEPC's mission includes promoting carbon projects, ensuring compliance with relevant norms and standards, and facilitating the registration and monitoring of these projects.

Project registration

All new carbon project developers in Benin must submit a registration request to the Autorité d’Enregistrement at least three weeks before submitting their validation report to a greenhouse gas certification program or relevant carbon standard. The request must include all required documentation for review.

Projects already certified or in the certification process when the decree was adopted must apply for registration within two months of its adoption.

The project document submitted for validation must include the following elements:

- Project description and development timeline

- Geographic area covered by the project

- Chosen greenhouse gas certification program or carbon standard

- Applied methodology

- Identification of stakeholders, including local communities, investors, and project developers

- Description of economic and social co-benefits

- Estimated greenhouse gas reductions and removals during the crediting period

- Proof of property rights or agreements with property owners related to the mitigation activity

- Stakeholder consultation details, including consent from local populations and communities

- Government authorizations, including environmental impact assessments and permits, if necessary

- Demonstration of project alignment with the Paris Agreement, Benin's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and relevant goals.

Carbon rights

- Beninese citizens, communities, and registered entities have the right to participate in the carbon market, including proposing and developing projects.

- All carbon credits generated by projects in Benin are sovereign assets.

- The state can assign or transfer carbon rights to private developers.

- The terms for transferring or conceding carbon rights will be set by a decree from the Minister of Finance, based on a proposal from the Autorité d'Enregistrement.

Participation in Article 6

- The government of Benin decides, at its discretion, to participate in mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to achieve emission reduction and other sustainable environmental goals.

- Private entities may be authorized to participate in these mechanisms after approval, based on criteria and guarantees set by the government.

- Emission reductions from carbon projects in Benin will contribute to the country’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

- The government will assess scenarios for applying corresponding adjustments in line with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, including relevant procedures, rules, and conditions.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Law 1819/2016 on tax deductions for renewables and carbon tax, regulated partially by Decree 926/2017 and last amended by Law 2169/2021
DESCRIPTION: Article 235-2 of the law deals with tax exemptions from January 10th, 2018, onward. Legal exceptions referred to in article 26 of the Tax Statute include (paragraph 7) the sale of electric power generated based on wind energy, biomass or agricultural waste, solar, geothermal or seas, according to the definitions of Law 1715 of 2014 and Decree 2755 of 2003, made only by generating companies, for a term of fifteen years, from the year 2017, provided that the following requirements are met: a) Process, obtain and sell certificates of emission of carbon dioxide in accordance with the terms of the Kyoto protocol; b) That at least 50% of the resources obtained from the sale of said certificates be invested in works of social benefit in the region where the generator operates. The investment that entitles the benefit will be made according to the proportion of each municipality affected by the construction and operation of the generating plant. Part nine of the law (articles 221 to 223) also institutes a national carbon tax. This was added by Decree 1625 /2016. Then, Decree 926/2017 regulated the procedure to certify being carbon neutral, in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 3 of article 221.The Law 2169/2021 amended this piece of legislation by stating the specific allocation of the National Carbon Tax (from fiscal year 2023 onward). The amendment outlined that 50% of the revenue will be allocated to mitigation and adaptation practices, such as coastal erosion management, reducing and monitoring deforestation, protection, preservation, restoration, and sustainable use of strategic areas and ecosystems, particularly páramos (high-altitude ecosystems), Payment for Environmental Services (PES), and funding measures for climate action as defined in the law and in Colombia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to the UNFCCC. Moreover, also stated that 50% of the revenue will go towards financing the National Integral Program for the Substitution of Illicit Crops (PNIS).

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National steel policy
DESCRIPTION: the Government has come out with National Steel Policy 2017 on 8th May, 2017, to facilitate faster growth and development of steel industry in the country. The policy envisages to domestically meet the entire demand of steel and high grade automotive steel, electrical steel, special steel and alloys for strategic applications. The policy projects crude steel capacity of 300 million tonnes (MT), production of 255 MT and a robust finished steel per capita consumption of 158 Kgs by 2030-31, as against the current consumption of 61 Kgs.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Ministerial Decree 294/2024 establishing the National System for the Certification of the Sustainability of Biofuels
DESCRIPTION: The Interministerial Decree of 7 August 2024 (DM n. 294/2024) establishes Italy’s national certification system for the sustainability of biocombustibles, as well as certification schemes for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO) and recycled carbon fuels (RCF). The decree implements the framework set out in Legislative Decree No. 199/2021 (transposing the EU Renewable Energy Directive – RED II) and defines the rules for verifying sustainability criteria, including minimum greenhouse-gas emission reductions, traceability along the supply chain through a mass-balance system, and certification procedures carried out by accredited bodies.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: LAW N° 2011/022 Of Governing the Electricity Sector in Cameroon
DESCRIPTION:
The law concerns the electricity sector, and is focused on ensuring its modernization and development.
 
 Part IV of the law sets out general goals for promoting renewable energy and energy efficiency, and for the use of renewables within the context of expanding rural electrification.
 
 The law states the government shall ensure the promotion and development of rural electrification nationwide, through connection to an interconnected network or through distributed generation. Within the general framework for increased electrification, priority is to be given to distributed generation from renewable sources (except when such sources are scarce, deficient or of high cost). The law allows for surplus electricity generated from renewable energy sources to be purchased by the transmission system operator or by local distributors.
 
 The law says that the State will ensure the promotion and development of renewable energy through establishing regulation for conditions and mechanisms for research, development, production of equipment and project financing. The government may also establish an agency to promote and develop renewable energy as and when necessary. The law also requires any electricity utility operate to connect renewable energy sources to networks (with connect fees borne by the applicant), with the conditions, volume and price for purchase of energy by utilities to be fixed by decree.
 
 The law calls for the implementation of energy efficiency measures in the industry, transport, commercial and residential sectors, and allows for the government to establish regulation for the obligations, conditions and resources necessary to implement such measures.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Fiji National Carbon Market Strategy Roadmap
DESCRIPTION:
This Strategy Roadmap provides an important overview of carbon market options, opportunities, risks, and priority actions which will help guide further policy development in Fiji and provides a basis for its interactions with new market-based opportunities. Carbon markets are meant to be an additional means to increase investment in sustainable development.

It is designed for use by policymakers, project developers, investors, land and resource owners, credit buyers, local communities, and other relevant stakeholders to shape their potential interaction with carbon market mechanisms.

It contains five chapters:

  • Chapter 1: A market vision, priorities and principles co-designed with multi- stakeholders.
  • Chapter 2: Fiji’s NDC targets, existing financing options, potential roles for high-integrity carbon markets, and the current state of play of carbon projects.
  • Chapter 3: Opportunities and risks, both general and specific to Fiji’s local contexts.
  • Chapter 4: Strategic considerations and options for engagement with carbon markets.
  • Chapter 5: Key pillar action items to enhance market readiness in Fiji, encompassing legal, governance, community benefits and landowner rights, partnerships, and finance.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Decree of 5 May 2011 - Incentivising Electricity Production from Photovoltaic Installations
DESCRIPTION:
Following the enactment of Legislative Decree 28/2011, Ministerial Decree 05/05/2011 (IV Energy Bill ) was published, which defined the incentive mechanism for plants that entered into operation after 31 May 2011. The aim was to align tariff levels with the evolution of photovoltaic technology costs and introduce a cumulative annual incentive cost limit of 6 billion euros.

As the cost limit identified by the IV Energy Bill approached, the Ministerial Decree of 05/07/2012 ( fifth Energy Bill ) was published, which partially confirmed the provisions set out in the Ministerial Decree of 05/05/2011 and set the cumulative cost of the incentives at 6.7 billion euros . The incentive provisions of the Energy Bill were no longer applied from 6 July 2013 after the ceiling of 6.7 billion euros was reached . The main purpose of this text is to support the production of electricity from renewable sources if different from photovoltaic, by implementing the sustainability of the costs of incentives as an adequate principle necessary for the promotion of the renewable energy sector (as previously implemented by the Legislative Decree 3 March 2011, n. 28, providing incentives for the production of electricity from plants with renewable sources other than photovoltaic).

It does not apply to new installations.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Honduras Biennial Update Report. BUR2; National Inventory Report (2016-2020)
Farm Competitiveness and Adaptation Plan 2014-2022
DESCRIPTION:
This Plan supports investments made by farms. The four priorities are livestock farming; economic and environmental performance for the plant sector; improving the energy performance of farms; and encouraging projects that are part of an agro-ecological approach.

Actions include modernising the production system; modifying the access to agricultural production factors and production conditions, taking into account the pressure of agricultural activity on natural resources and environments, as well as climate change; investing in fertilisers and plant protection products in line with agro-environmental and climate measures; and the development of organic farming. Apart from investment support, other measures include facilitation, advisory, training and cooperation.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Roadmap for Green Hydrogen
DESCRIPTION: This document sets the government's strategy to ramp up the production and use of low-carbon hydrogen in the country. It notably seeks to couple it to the production of renewable energy from solar and wind, and to establish an exporting industry for green hydrogen.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Regulation on Continuous Emission Measurement Systems
DESCRIPTION: This Regulation was set by the Ministry of Environment and Urban planning to outline the installation, operation, and establishment of continuous emission monitoring systems (CEMS). Relevant businesses/facilities have an obligation to install, calibrate, track, and report on their CEMS. The Regulation establishes the standard calculations for the CEMS, its reporting functions, testing, and conditions of its inspection. Authorised facilities with CEMS are subject to report reviews, on-site inspections, and potential administrative sanctions if their systems are non-compliant.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: 2022-2030 Environmental Protection and Climate Change Management Development Programme
DESCRIPTION: The Environmental Protection and Climate Change Management Development Programme outlines a wide range of challenges and potential measures for mitigating and adapting to climate change over the 2022-2030 time period. A particular emphasis in the programme is on the challenges posed by inefficient heat use in the buildings sector, which reduces the climate benefits of existing renewables deployment by inflating overall energy demand. Other issues the programme articulates include lack of trained personnel in the green sector, and poor transparency of climate risk and mitigation data. It calls for improved training, governance and regulatory enforcement in a range of sectors.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: The food sector in a changing climate — a plan for what the Swedish National Food Agency needs to do
DESCRIPTION:
The Swedish National Food Agency believes that the goals in Agenda 2030 and Sweden's national environmental goals should be guiding for climate adaptation work in the food sector. Many of the goals in Agenda 2030 concern food consumption and food security. Goal 13 explicitly includes climate adaptation. Reduced food waste (Goal 12) contributes to reduced pressure on food production and thus indirectly contributes to the food sector's climate adaptation. The goal of sustainable consumption and production patterns (Goal 12), the goal of securing food supply and improved nutrition (Goal 2) and the goal of access to water (Goal 6) also have strong links to climate adaptation. The generation goal is a strategic goal that should permeate the entire national environmental goal work. The food sector is affected to a greater or lesser extent by all environmental quality goals. Eight of the sixteen goals have been identified by the Swedish National Food Agency as particularly relevant. These are:

  • Limited climate impact,
  • A non-toxic environment,
  • No eutrophication,
  • Living lakes and watercourses,
  • Good quality groundwater,
  • A balanced sea and a living coast and archipelago,
  • A rich agricultural landscape and
  • A rich flora and fauna.

The Swedish National Food Agency contributes to developing a long-term sustainable and robust food sector that actively addresses climate change through knowledge building, surveys, scientific risk assessments and the dissemination of knowledge to public and private activities.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Action plan to produce 1 million heat pumps in France
DESCRIPTION:
This Action Plan supports the transitiojn to cleaner energy. Heat accounts for 45% of final energy consumption in France, and only 27% of this heat will come from renewable sources in 2022. Building heating remains a significant source of fossil fuel consumption (oil and especially gas).

The production of air-to-water heat pumps, a dynamic RD ecosystem, a building stock with a well-developed hot water network, and access to affordable, carbon-free electricity, enables French production sites to quickly adapt to growing demand. High-efficiency heat pumps and air conditioners will be adapted to refrigerants with low Global Warming Potential (GWP).

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Wildlife Strategy 2030
DESCRIPTION:
Kenya's National Wildlife Strategy 2030 is based on four pillars:
  1. Resilient Ecosystems
  2. Engagement by all Kenyans
  3. Evidence based Decision Making
  4. Sustainability and Governance
It recognises that climate change places Kenya's wildlife at risk, but also that ecosystem conservation and management can contribute to greater climate resilience by serving as a form of adaptation. It specifically calls for the creation of a National Wildlife Adaptation Strategy, which would determine complementarities between wildlife conservation and climate change adaptation.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Long-term Strategy on Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reductions
DESCRIPTION:
This Strategy sets out sector-specific and technology pathways to reaching Ireland's 2050 climate targets.


A key objective of the Strategy is to clarify sectoral adjustments required to reach net zero by 2050 and support policy stability and investment in the medium- and long-term.


The Strategy contains measures categorised according to the degree of certainty around their use and suitability to realise 2030 and 2050 targets.


Core measures include technologies and measures that already exist today and could deliver substantial emissions reduction. Those focus on delivering a renewable electricity system; GHG-efficient agricultural practices; electrification in transport, built environment, and industry; restoration of forestry and peatlands; fuel substitution; and a circular economy.


Further measures are those technologies and measures that are technologically more challenging or not yet available at scale but required to deliver the climate targets. Such measures are aimed at accelerating a sustainable transformation in agriculture and deploy zero-emission gas.


Alternative-further measures are those technologies which currently exist at research or pilot stage or have not reached commercial scale, such as radical demand reduction (e.g. aviation) and deploy carbon capture and storage in the industry sector.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Green ODA strategy
DESCRIPTION: • The Green ODA Strategy supports the green transition and carbon neutrality in developing countries. It enhances South Korea’s leadership on the issue, increasing contributions to green-related international organisations including the Green Climate Fund and the Global Green Growth Institute, and expanding partnerships with UN agencies and multilateral development banks.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Presidential Decree No. 22-122 creating a High Energy Council
DESCRIPTION: The Council decides on the strategies to be followed with regard to the country’s energy security, especially through preserving, renewing and developing national reserves of hydrocarbons, following up and evaluating the implementation of long-term plans to develop the basic structures for the production, transport, supply, storage and distribution of energy materials and the development of new and renewable energies. The Council also decided on strategies regarding the energy transition towards a new national model for energy production and consumption.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: The Barbados Sustainable Development Policy
DESCRIPTION:
The National Sustainable Development (NSD) Policy of 2004 is a product of the National Commission on Sustainable Development (NCSD) that was established by Cabinet directive on March 30th, 1997 with a mandate to develop a National Sustainable Development Policy for Barbados. The NSD is a broad document addressing the socially, environmental and economic sustainability aspects in order to issue governmental strategies forward and sensitise Barbadians to sustainable development.




The Policy includes a series climate-related recommendations including in transport, agriculture, forestry, energy production and use, including energy efficiency and renewables and buildings. It further encourages Caribbean and regional cooperation, sensitises over the gender question in sustainable policies, and coastal and marine preservation. Indicators for sustainable development shall also be elaborated.
KEYWORDS: Energy Demand;Energy Supply;Institutions / Administrative Arrangements;REDD+ And LULUCF;Research And Development;Transport

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Ministerial Accord No. 089 on Regulation for NAMAs
DESCRIPTION: The Decree establishes the National Authority for Implementation of Nationally Appropriate Mitigation Actions (NAMAs) developed in co-ordination with the UNDP. This Authority is chaired by the Minister of Environment while the Undersecretary of Climate Change is in charge of implementing the registry. PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Decree UP-106 On the Establishment of The Climate Council Under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan

The Energy and Climate Plan addresses all five dimensions of the EU Energy Union: decarbonisation, energy efficiency, energy security, internal energy markets and research, innovation and competitiveness. The plan establishes key objectives : 1) to accelerate the transition from traditional fuels to renewable sources by promoting the gradual phasing out of coal for electricity generation in favour of an electricity mix based on a growing share of renewables; 2) to implement policies and measures in order to reduce greenhouse gases (phase out of coal, higher CO2 price, acceleration of renewables and energy efficiency in manufacturing process level); 3) to use a mix of fiscal, economic, regulatory and policy instruments to ensure an energy efficiency; 4) to become less dependent on imports by increasing renewable sources and energy efficiency and to diversify sources of supply through the use of natural gas, including liquefied natural gas (LNG); 5) to ensure a greater degree of market integration and the development of processes, products and knowledge for the use of renewables, energy efficiency and network technology.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Transport Canada’s Climate Change Adaptation Plan 2021/22 to 2025/26
DESCRIPTION:
Transport Canada's Climate Change Adaptation Plan 2021/22 to 2025/26 is a five-year plan designed to build the department's climate resilience and support broader adaptation efforts across the Canadian transportation sector.

The main goals of the plan are to:

  • Goal 1: Strengthen internal knowledge and capacity: This focuses on educating Transport Canada employees and teams about climate risks and opportunities, enabling them to take adaptation actions in their work. It includes learning activities, identifying information gaps, and sharing knowledge.
  • Goal 2: Embed climate change considerations: This aims to integrate climate considerations into Transport Canada's corporate planning, decision-making tools, regulatory processes, programs, plans, and strategies.
  • Goal 3: Understand climate change impacts on the transportation system: This goal supports Transport Canada's ability to maintain a safe, secure, efficient, and environmentally responsible transportation system despite evolving climate change impacts. Activities include cost-benefit analyses of adaptation and research on co-benefits of climate mitigation and adaptation in the transportation sector.
  • Goal 4: Demonstrate continued leadership in transportation adaptation: This involves Transport Canada's ongoing engagement with domestic and international forums, leveraging partnerships, and exchanging knowledge to optimize its adaptation outcomes and contribute its expertise to the field of transportation adaptation

This plan is "evergreen," allowing for continuous integration of new or evolving climate risks and opportunities over its five-year span. It also contributes to the department's integrated risk management efforts.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Carbon Market Framework
DESCRIPTION:
Malawi's Carbon Market Framework outlines structured approach to carbon market engagement, by providing clear guidelines and setting up procedures for participation in the mechanism. The framework also outlines how the institutional arrangements have been set up, along with clear fees structure.

Institutional Arrangements

- Ministry of Natural Resources and Climate Change (MNRCC): The MNRCC acts as the Authorizing Entity (AE) for all carbon market projects in Malawi. It is responsible for authorizing Mitigation Outcomes (MOs) and providing policy direction.

- Environmental Affairs Department (EAD): The EAD is the Designated National Authority (DNA) for carbon trading and is the entry point for all carbon market projects. It oversees carbon market transactions, manages a Carbon Registry, and is responsible for compliance, approvals, and reporting. The EAD also hosts the Carbon Market Office to support project developers and investors.

- National Steering Committee on Climate Change (NSCCC): This committee provides policy direction, oversight, and guidance on all matters related to international carbon markets.

- Mitigation Expert Working Group (MEWG): This group provides technical advice and recommendations to the DNA on which projects are eligible to participate in carbon markets, ensuring they align with Malawi's priorities and the ambition of its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

Malawi’s Mitigation Activity Development Cycle

The development cycle for mitigation activities in Malawi is a multi-step process managed by the EAD and MNRCC.

- Article 6.2 and VCM:

The process will involve:

- MAP Registration: The MAP registers with the MCRS to get a unique identification number (MAP-ID).

- MAIN Submission: The MAP submits a Mitigation Activity Idea Note (MAIN).

- Review and No Objection: The EAD reviews the MAIN and, if it is approved, issues a Letter of No Objection.

- MADD Validation: The MAP develops a Mitigation Activity Design Document (MADD), which is then validated by an accredited Validation/Verification Body (VVB).

- Authorization and Registration: The EAD reviews the positive validation report, and upon payment of an administrative fee, issues a Letter of Authorization (LOA) and registers the activity in the MCRS.

- Monitoring and Verification: The MAP monitors the activity and submits a monitoring report for verification by an eligible VVB.

- Issuance and Transfer: Upon a positive review of the verification report by the EAD and payment of an issuance fee, the MOs are issued. The EAD retains a portion of the MOs for the National Buffer Account and transfers the rest to the acquiring party.

- Article 6.4:The cycle for Article 6.4 activities is similar but operates under the supervision of the UNFCCC and its rules. This includes a global stakeholder consultation and validation by a UNFCCC-accredited Designated Operating Entity (DOE).

Requirements for Mitigation Activity Development

- Eligible Activities: Activities must contribute to Malawi's conditional NDC mitigation targets, respect human rights, and align with sustainable development goals. The framework includes a positive list of eligible activities across various sectors (Energy, IPPU, Waste, Agriculture) and a negative list of ineligible activities, such as those under Malawi's unconditional NDC scope or that use nuclear energy.

- Methodologies and Standards: Malawi pre-approves methodologies from international standards like the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), Gold Standard (GS), and VERRA's Verified Carbon Standard (VCS).

- Verification and Validation Bodies (VVBs): VVBs must be registered in the MCRS and accredited by recognized international standards. UNFCCC-recognized DOEs are also eligible to validate Article 6.4 projects.

Fees and Share of Proceeds (SOPs)

Malawi has a fee structure to cover administrative costs and a Share of Proceeds (SOP) to fund adaptation and mitigation activities.

- Fees Levels:

- Administrative Fees: A total of USD 11,000 for Article 6 projects, which includes an application fee, review fees, and a registration/authorization fee. For VCM activities, MAP application fee of USD 1,000.00 for registration in the MCRS and its account maintenance.

- Listing Fees: USD 10,000 for VCM activities requiring Corresponding Adjustment and USD 7,500 for Article 6.4 projects.

- VVB Fees: USD 1,000 for VVB registration and a USD 500 application fee per project.

- MO Issuance Fee: USD 0.20 per MO.

- Corresponding Adjustment Fee: USD 4 per issued MO.

- Concessional Fees: Periodic payment for using public property and assets.

- Non-Monetary Fees:

- Buffer Fee: A 5% retention of issued MOs for Article 6.2 and VCM projects with a CA, and a 1% retention for Article 6.4 projects. These retained MOs are placed in a National Buffer Account to reduce over-crediting risks and for Malawi's own NDC achievement.

- Share of Proceeds (SOPs): The SOP is a monetary fee collected from mitigation activities with a Corresponding Adjustment. The revenue from SOPs is shared among key stakeholders at the national and local levels. The amount varies depending on the project type:

- Technology-based projects: 15% to 40% of gross revenue, depending of the type of activity implemented.

- Land-based projects: 15% for customary land and 25% for public protected land.

- Non-Compliance mechanism (VCM projects not requiring corresponding Adjustment): 25% of gross revenue from Certified Emission Reductions.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Response Plan with a Multi-Threat and Health Approach 2020
DESCRIPTION:
In 2008, the Government of Reconciliation and National Unity (GRUN) presented the National Response Plan (PNR) as a regulatory instrument of SINAPRED reference for the coordination of response plans, as well as for the development of policies, strategies, conceptual and methodological instruments that allow for the generation of common planning for all response actors at the institutional, sectoral, and territorial levels. In light of the achievements and progress of the last 12 years, a new version of the National Response Plan is being presented, updated and in line with the state of risk management in our country.

This document is organized into 10 chapters. The first three are introductory and contextual aspects (this Introduction, Regulatory Framework, and Objectives). This is followed, in a logical order, by the definition of scenarios from a multi-hazard approach, the national response organization, alert systems, the sectoral and institutional response strategy, activation of the National Risk Management Plan (PNR), and support systems and resources. A chapter on post-disaster recovery concludes the PNR, emphasizing that pre-disaster recovery planning and preparation must occur alongside response preparation, and highlighting progress and prospects for strengthening this aspect of comprehensive risk management.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: A policy framework for climate and energy in the period from 2020 to 2030
DESCRIPTION: To ensure that the EU is on the cost-effective track towards meeting its objective of cutting emissions by at least 80% by 2050, the Commission proposed the '2030 framework for climate change and energy policies'. It was adopted by the European Council in October 2014 as a strategic document, although binding legislation is yet to be drafted. It includes the binding 2030 EU domestic GHG reduction target of at least 40% compared to 1990, as well as a target of at least 27% for final renewable energy, and a at least 27% for energy savings by 2030 (target to be reviewed upwards to 30% in 2020). In addition, the EU ETS is to be reformed and strengthened. To achieve the 2030 binding 40% reduction target, the sectors covered by the EU ETS would have to reduce their emissions by 43% compared to 2005. In parallel, emissions from non-EU ETS sectors would need to be cut by 30% below the 2005 level, through national measures. To address the surplus of emission allowances in the EU ETS and to improve the system's resilience, a market stability reserve is to be established and the annual factor to reduce the cap on the maximum permitted emissions is to be changed from the current 1.74% to 2.2% from 2021. The volume of free allowances is to be reduced progressively; Member States with a GDP per capita below 60% of the EU average may opt to continue to give free allowances to the energy sector up to 2030, but the maximum amount handed out for free after 2020 should be no more than 40% of the allowances allocated to eligible Member States. The 2030 Framework stresses the importance of a fully functioning and connected EU energy market, as foreseen in the European Energy Security Strategy (2014). The Commission is to be supported by Member States to take measures to ensure achievement of a minimum target of 10% of electricity interconnections no later than 2020. The 2030 framework also launches the preparation of the Energy Union aiming at affordable, secure and sustainable energy, by 'pooling resources, connecting networks and uniting member states' power when negotiating with non EU countries'. Specific legislative proposals are expected in 2015.

DESCRIPTION:

The executive branch of government may update the tax rate annually, and may increase the rate in accordance with any variation established by the Consumer Price Index. The tax applies to all liquid fuels, with the exception of jet fuel. Sales of fuel to manufacturers of gasoline, for the purposes of producing gasoline, are also exempted from the tax. The carbon tax rate for 2022 is UYU 5,645.45 (approximately USD 137.29).

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Armenia’s Climate Law
DESCRIPTION:
This climate law establishes Armenia’s overall legal framework for addressing climate change and organizing climate policy across the country in line with the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, covering both mitigation and adaptation. Its main purpose is to create a coordinated national system for both mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions and alligning national action with international commitments) and adaptation by helping society, infrastructure, and the economy prepare for and respond to climate impacts. The law defines responsibilities across government institutions and encourages cooperation between national authorities, local governments, businesses, and individuals. It introduces mechanisms for climate planning, implementation, monitoring, reporting, and evaluation to improve accountability and transparency. The law also supports the development of financing mechanisms and creates institutional arrangements for coordinated climate action, establishes a national measurement, reporting, and verification system, and integrates climate finance into the public financial management system.

Key policy instruments include Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), a long-term low-emission development strategy, and a national climate adaptation programme, all approved by Government. The law introduces regulatory tools such as GHG emission permits, carbon pricing mechanisms (carbon tax or emissions trading), and mandatory GHG accounting and reporting by legal entities above defined thresholds. A measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) system aligned with the Paris Agreement's Enhanced Transparency Framework is established, with annual government reporting to the National Assembly. Lastly, Chapter 4 creates a Climate Council as the central coordination and advisory body. Chaired by a Deputy Prime Minister, the Council brings together representatives of relevant government bodies, civil society organisations, scientific institutions and local authorities. Its mandate includes reviewing national climate documents (NDCs, strategies, adaptation programmes), issuing recommendations to the Government, and ensuring cross-sectoral coordination of climate policy.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Recovery and resilience plan for Romania
DESCRIPTION:
To benefit from the support of the Recovery and Resilience Facility set up by the EU in the aftermath of the COVID-19-induced economic crisis, Member States submit their recovery and resilience plans to the European Commission. Each plan sets out the reforms and investments to be implemented by end-2026 and Member States can receive financing up to a previously agreed allocation. Each plan should effectively address challenges identified in the European Semester, particularly the country-specific recommendations of 2019 and 2020 adopted by the Council. It should also advance the green and digital transitions and make Member States’ economies and societies more resilient. The Commission validates the plan after which it effectively enters in force and EU subsidies can start flowing towards the member state. As of March 28th, 2022, the Implementing Decision has not been released.


41% of the plan’s total allocation for reforms and investments supports climate objectives. 
  •  Railway modernisation: modernising railway infrastructure, including electrified or zero-emission railways and rolling stock. €3.9 billion
  • Urban mobility: infrastructure for a green and more secure urban transport. €1.8 billion
  • Clean energy production: phasing-out of coal and lignite power production, deployment of renewables as well as related production processes, and hydrogen. €855 million
  •  Energy efficiency of buildings: energy-efficient renovation and seismic renovation of buildings to reduce CO2 emissions by at least 0.15 million tons in private buildings and 0.075 million tons in public buildings. €2.7 billion
  • Biodiversity and environmental protection: afforestation and reforestation and forest nurseries, as well as other biodiversity measures for ecological reconstruction and species protection. €1.1 billion

In its plan, Romania indicates that it aims to exit coal by 2032, and that it will legislate on the future of mines, jobs and socio-economic support by mid 2022.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Royal Decree 376 establishing the Spanish Office for Climate Change
DESCRIPTION:
The Spanish Office of Climate Change (Oficina Española de Cambio Climático) was established by Royal Decree 376/2001 as a collegiate body within the Ministry of Environment, now known as the Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge. This decree consolidated climate-related responsibilities, previously dispersed across various government bodies, and tasked the Office with coordinating and implementing climate change policies, monitoring international agreements, and fostering collaboration with regional governments and stakeholders.
Subsequent royal decrees have restructured and elevated the status of the Office. Royal Decree 1000/2003 transformed it into a sub-directorate under the General Secretariat of the Environment, reflecting the growing importance of climate change in Spain's environmental policies. Royal Decree 1477/2004 further restructured the Ministry, establishing the Secretariat General for the Prevention of Pollution and Climate Change, under which the Office operates as a sub-directorate. The Office's functions now include advancing national climate policies, aligning with international frameworks, and integrating climate change considerations across sectors.
The most recent development is Royal Decree 503/2024, which updates the structure of the Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge, emphasising its central role in climate change mitigation and adaptation. The Ministry aims to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, in line with the European Green Deal, through policies targeting greenhouse gas emission reductions, energy transition, and biodiversity protection. The Spanish Office of Climate Change, now under the Ministry's Secretariat of State for the Environment, leads the formulation of national climate policies, promotes citizen participation, and coordinates with regional governments. The Ministry's holistic approach addresses demographic challenges, ensures sustainable development across sectors, and oversees strategic energy planning, demonstrating a comprehensive commitment to Spain's ecological and climate-related challenges.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Climate and Environmental Strategy for the ICT Sector
DESCRIPTION:
The Ministry of Transport and Communications appointed a working group in November 2019 to draw up a climate and environmental strategy for the information and communication technology sector (ICT sector). The task of the working group was to establish a common view on the climate and environmental impacts of the ICT sector in Finland and to recommend means to manage the impacts. The working group published an interim report that gave a broad and comprehensive picture of the situation in terms of the climate and environmental impacts of the ICT sector in June 2020 and the final report including recommendations for measures in November 2020. To ensure a broad-based view, the final report was circulated for comments before the strategy was finalised.

The purpose of the national Climate and Environmental Strategy for the ICT Sector is to promote ecologically sustainable digitalisation and support the achievement of climate and environmental objectives. The Strategy presents recommendations for measures related to a climate- and environment-friendly ICT infrastructure and data economy, sustainable material flows and a circular economy, expanding the knowledge base and developing the measurement framework, enhancing consumer awareness and expertise, and utilising emerging technologies and responding to challenges.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: National Environmental Restoration Program 2025-2030 (Programa Nacional de Restauración Ambiental 2025-2030)
DESCRIPTION: The National Environmental Restoration Program 2025-2030 is a national policy in Mexico, established to address the country's extensive environmental degradation and biodiversity loss. It represents a commitment from the Mexican government to a "humanist environmental policy," which views environmental restoration as fundamental to both social well-being and ecological justice. The programme outlines a long-term approach to restoring degraded ecosystems across the country, from urban parks and agricultural lands to protected natural areas. Drawing inspiration from the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the PNRA prioritises harmonising, organising, and scaling up restoration efforts, which were previously fragmented, through a series of phased objectives and targets for various ecosystems.In the context of climate change, the PNRA is framed as an instrument for both mitigation and adaptation. The policy aims to contribute to Mexico's national and international climate commitments, including the target of a 35% reduction in GHG emissions by 2030. This is to be achieved through large-scale ecosystem restoration projects, such as restoring 100,000 hectares of forest ecosystems and achieving net-zero deforestation by 2030. Furthermore, the programme seeks to reduce the vulnerability of the population to the impacts of climate change by strengthening communities' adaptive capacity through environmental restoration. It also commits to developing a National Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation Plan that integrates restoration and nature-based solutions as key strategies.

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Resolution 290/2021 on the National Program to Strengthen the Circular Economy

PRINCIPAL_TITLE: Sustainable Development and Inclusive Growth Strategy SDDCI-Niger 2035
